195.bp: Video platforms like TikTok face a ranking problem: which video should you see next? The obvious answer—show the most-watched videos—works in the moment, but platforms care about your lifetime value (how long you stay, how often you return over weeks or months). These are two different targets, and only long-term value predicts whether users stick around. This paper tackles the hard practical version: predicting long-term value in production systems that serve billions of videos daily.
195.wh: Long-term value prediction faces three specific obstacles. First, the position where a video appears (top of feed vs. middle) affects engagement; users see videos higher up more, so a video's high watch count might just mean it was positioned well, not that it's truly engaging. Second, when multiple videos influence your stay (you watched three clips, which one kept you?), it's unclear which deserves credit for your long-term value. Third, engagement signals arrive over days or weeks; systems must make ranking decisions now with incomplete data.
195.ap: The paper introduces three concrete fixes. For position bias, they build a module that looks at the distribution of engagement across positions (some videos always perform well whether top or middle; others only shine when promoted) and normalizes signals accordingly. For credit assignment, they train a model that learns how much each video's context, your past behavior, and the video's content each contribute to keeping you engaged—avoiding hand-coded rules. They also filter noise explicitly so causality is clearer. For time, they track per-creator patterns day-by-day and model when users return because a creator re-engages them.
195.ww: Position-aware normalization works because it separates signal from placement luck: if a video does well everywhere, it's truly good, not privileged. Multi-dimensional attribution captures the real mechanisms—context matters, user habit matters, content matters—and learning their weights beats human guesses. Creator modeling works because users don't engage uniformly over time; some creators keep people coming back weeks later, and that's a real pattern to learn.
195.po: In production systems at billion-scale, this means the ranking model can predict which videos to show you now because they'll keep you engaged next month, not just this hour. The framework handles delayed feedback (data arrives late), cleans noisy signals, and runs on real platforms, making long-term value a practical lever for user retention rather than an academic ideal.

196.bp: Tor's whole purpose is to hide your web traffic so no one can see which websites you visit—a lifeline for journalists and activists in repressive places. But security researchers discovered you can identify which websites someone visits just by watching the *shape and timing* of their encrypted traffic, even if you can't decrypt it. This paper shows an attack that works even when someone does something realistic: opening multiple websites at once.
196.wh: Traffic analysis is like listening to a phone call in a foreign language you don't understand; you can't hear the words, but you notice one voice gets loud then quiet, another interrupts. Previous attacks assumed one person was browsing one website. Real life: someone opens five tabs, streaming a video, reading news, shopping. All this traffic mixes together, and it becomes much harder to say 'this spike was from Gmail and this one was from YouTube.' The attacker doesn't know how many tabs are even open.
196.ap: This work borrows an idea from audio engineering: the 'cocktail party problem' (how a human picks out one conversation in a noisy room). They reframe multi-tab traffic as a mixing problem: separate the traffic signals without knowing how many sources there are. They treat the mixed network traffic like a recording of overlapping voices and decompose it into individual streams. Then they classify each stream by watching patterns across time (a Gmail login flows differently than a YouTube video) and frequency (does the traffic spike every 100ms or smoothly?).
196.ww: Blind source separation works here because each website's traffic has a fingerprint—Gmail logins are bursty and short, YouTube is steady and long, Google Docs has pauses when you're typing. Even when mixed, the patterns remain consistent enough to untangle. The time-frequency trick captures this: different sites have different rhythms, and you can exploit those rhythms even when everything is mixed together.
196.po: The result: an attacker can now identify which websites you visit via Tor even when you're opening multiple sites at once, with 78.6% accuracy improvement over prior methods. This reveals a real privacy vulnerability in multi-tab browsing—it matters for Tor's promise of anonymity and suggests new defenses are needed.

197.bp: Banks that serve poor communities rely on web platforms to approve credit quickly. A credit card fraud—someone using a stolen card—directly harms vulnerable people who can already barely access credit. The system must catch fraud while approving legitimate users, but small banks have little data compared to tech giants. Meanwhile, malicious actors might try to poison the system itself by inserting hidden triggers into the machine-learning model during updates, making it approve fraudulent transactions no matter what.
197.wh: Small web banks face a real trap. They need machine learning to spot fraud, but fraud detection only improves with large datasets—and they don't have them. Sharing data across banks (federated learning) helps, but it creates a new vulnerability: during the aggregation step where multiple banks' model improvements get merged, a malicious bank could inject a 'backdoor' (a secret pattern that triggers when seen, like 'approve transactions with amount=4444'). The system wouldn't detect it because aggregate models look clean at first glance. Meanwhile, real fraud is rare, making it harder to learn from the few examples present.
197.ap: The paper proposes a defense-attack co-design. The attack side: bad actors use reinforcement learning (a technique that learns to win games) to evolve their backdoor trigger over time, making it stealthier while staying effective—this tests how good defenses are. The defense side: after each model merge, the system runs a selection-evaluation cycle, checking whether something suspicious happened (checking for trigger patterns) and adapting to block them. On the normal detection side, they use privacy-preserving methods to share features across banks without revealing raw data, and a contrastive learning approach (learning by comparing fraudulent vs. legitimate transactions) to work with few examples.
197.ww: The federated setup works because small banks together have enough data, and privacy methods mean they don't expose customer information. Contrastive learning works for scarce fraud data because you learn by comparing pairs: 'this transaction is similar to known fraud, that one isn't.' The adaptive defense works because adversaries can't stay ahead if the system watches, detects changes, and adjusts the filter in a closed loop.
197.po: The framework lets small web banks detect fraud with the combined strength of many banks' data while staying private and resistant to backdoor attacks. It's explicitly designed for the extreme scarcity that small banks face, making inclusive financial infrastructure more secure.

198.bp: During a disaster—earthquake, flood, hurricane—people post images and text on social media asking for help: 'missing person,' 'road blocked,' 'power out.' Rescue teams need to automatically sort these by urgency and type. But the system must explain its decisions because decisions affect real people's lives—if the algorithm says 'this is low priority,' someone might not see it. Explaining images is harder than explaining text; an algorithm can point to words in a tweet, but pointing to 'which part of this photo matters?' is unclear.
198.wh: Image explanation is hard because a human can't easily verify why a model paid attention to a particular part of the photo; it might have just learned a shortcut (certain pixel colors = disaster category). Text explanation is easier: point to a word, anyone can verify it's relevant. The naive approach is to explain text and ignore images, but images carry crucial information in disasters—'is this building damaged?' or 'is this person visible?' Both modalities are needed, but the annotation burden (having humans label why each image belongs to a category) is enormous.
198.ap: Instead of labeling image rationales directly, the paper uses text as a bridge. Step one: extract explanation words from the tweet (e.g., 'missing' and 'stranded' explain the 'displaced persons' category). Step two: map those text explanations to image patches (regions of the photo) through a visual-language model—a system trained on aligned image-text pairs. The map learns 'when the text says missing, this photo region matters.' Step three: classify based on both extracted rationales. The trick is using the text as supervision for the image, saving human annotation effort.
198.ww: This works because aligned image-text models have learned deep correspondences—they know that certain words relate to certain visual features. By leveraging this pre-learned alignment, you can transfer the text explanation to images without new human labeling. The joint representation ensures text and image rationales point to the same underlying meaning.
198.po: The result: a classification system that explains both text and image decisions (showing which tweet words and photo regions support the category) with 2–35% better accuracy than baselines. In disasters, this means rescue teams can trust and quickly verify why a post was categorized, and annotation cost drops dramatically because you label text once and get image explanations for free.

199.bp: Large language models (LLMs) are becoming tools for everything, but they're huge—hundreds of billions of numbers describing patterns in text—and running them requires expensive data centers. A natural question: can we shrink them to fit on a phone or edge device? Quantization is a technique for this: use fewer bits to store each number (8 bits instead of 16, or 4 instead of 8). The catch: even tiny quantized models require many multiply-accumulate operations (the core math of neural networks), and on a battery-powered device, that math drains power fast.
199.wh: Standard quantization has two problems. First, after reducing the precision of numbers, the model still does dense matrix multiplication (every weight × every activation), which is inherently expensive on mobile chips. Second, uniform bit-widths are wasteful: some weight values are big and important, others small and forgettable, but standard quantization treats them the same. You could use lower precision for unimportant values, but current hardware doesn't support mixed-precision storage in a practical way.
199.ap: The paper proposes SpikeQuant, inspired by how brains work. Biological brains use spiking—neurons send brief electrical pulses. This paper translates that idea to quantization: represent activations (the values flowing through the network) as binary spike counts instead of continuous numbers. Think of it like: instead of storing 5.7, you store 'fire 6 times.' The key insight is that important (salient) activation values get higher precision (more spikes), while unimportant values get lower precision. The model then does accumulation instead of multiplication—summing up spike counts is far cheaper than multiplying floating-point numbers. The quantization scale is embedded into the spike threshold, so no separate rescaling step is needed.
199.ww: Binary spikes are energy-efficient because counting is cheaper than multiplication. Mixed-precision storage works because different values need different bit-widths, and spike counts naturally encode this. Eliminating explicit dequantization (rescaling) removes extra operations that cost latency and power on edge devices. Brain-like computation is a good fit because nature has been solving this problem (how to compute with limited energy) for millions of years.
199.po: The result is a path to running large language models on phones and embedded devices without the usual energy cost. Fewer multiply-accumulate operations and mixed precision mean faster, lower-power inference—making LLM capabilities available on battery-powered hardware, not just data centers.

200.bp: When you search 'pizza near me,' a search engine like Google or Baidu returns results. But 'near me' means something different to each person—you might be looking for a specific style, or near your office rather than home. Pure keyword matching can't capture your specific intent. Personalized search rewrites your query before searching, transforming 'pizza' into 'vegan pizza within 3km of Zhongguancun' based on your history and profile. This is powerful but requires understanding intent from your behavior, and doing that reasoning fast enough for real-time search is a challenge.
200.wh: Large language models can reason about intent well—they understand context and nuance—but adding reasoning steps (called Chain-of-Thought, where the model explicitly shows its reasoning) to every search query is too slow. A production search engine needs to rewrite and return results in milliseconds; adding reasoning overhead makes queries lag. Without reasoning, the model makes quick but shallow choices. The tension is fundamental: thinking deeply takes time, but search engines can't wait.
200.ap: PicQue uses a two-stage training approach. Stage one: train the model using a hybrid method where examples include both the reasoning steps (how to think about your intent) and the rewritten query. During training, the model learns to do both; during deployment, you skip the reasoning part and just decode the rewritten query. This is like a student who practices showing all homework steps in class, then on a test just writes the answer without showing work—but the reasoning process improved their intuition, so the answer is still correct. Stage two: reinforce the pipeline by training on real user interactions—which rewrites actually led to people clicking results.
200.ww: Hybrid supervised fine-tuning works because the model learns the reasoning internally (in its weights) even if it doesn't output reasoning at test time. The chain-of-thought examples in training inject reasoning capability, and the model compresses that capability into direct decoding. This is much faster than generating reasoning text on every query. Reinforcement learning from click data ensures the rewrites actually match what users want.
200.po: The system achieves high accuracy (the rewrites are semantically correct) with low latency (milliseconds, not seconds), making personalized query rewriting practical for real search engines at scale. It handles the real challenge: inferring personal intent from behavior and encoding it into the search automatically.

201.bp: Advertising platforms host billions of ads daily. Scammers use AI to generate fake ads at scale—deepfake videos, synthetic speech, photoshopped images—luring people into cryptocurrency schemes or fake shops. A naive detection approach looks at each image or video alone: 'is this image fake?' But scammers don't launch one ad; they launch thousands of near-identical variants with slight tweaks, rotating them to evade detection. To stop this, you need to see the campaign as a system, not individual assets.
201.wh: Asset-level detection (analyzing one ad image) misses the scam because scammers rely on volume and rotation. They generate a core template (say, a fake celebrity video), create hundreds of slight variations (different frame crops, added text, re-encoded to bypass fingerprinting), and publish them across many fake accounts on rotating schedules. By the time a system flags one variant, the scammer switches to another. The system also uses auxiliary content (e.g., a 'educational disclaimer' video) that masks the actual scam, making individual assets look legitimate in isolation.
201.ap: This paper reconstructs entire scam campaigns layer by layer. They trace back from a detected scam ad to find all related ads, accounts, and timelines. They identify patterns: stable 'persuasion schemes' (the core lie, like 'get rich quick'), production templates (how the scammer assembles the ad), and variant generation strategies (how they make thousands of nearly-identical versions). They observe that audio—especially synthetic speech—is the dominant persuasive channel, while visuals range from montage to fully synthetic. Crucially, they document the temporal deployment: ads burst on a schedule and rotate, suggesting an automated workflow.
201.ww: Campaigns have structure that individual assets don't. A genuine ad might vary in some ways, but scam campaigns have mass production patterns, auxiliary masking content, and bursts on schedules. These patterns are harder to fake than a single convincing ad. By recognizing the structure—'this template is being cloned 5,000 times across accounts'—detection can catch the whole campaign, not chase variants forever.
201.po: The result is a framework for campaign-level detection: systems should look for production templates, deployment patterns, and temporal rotation, not just asset properties. Mitigation can now block at the campaign level (suspend the template) rather than playing whack-a-mole with variants. For advertising platforms, this shifts the arms race toward structure detection, which is more resilient.

202.bp: Fine-tuning is the standard way to adapt a pre-trained large language model (LLM) to a specific task: you take GPT or LLaMA and train it on your data. Pure fine-tuning updates billions of weights, which is expensive. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is a trick: instead of updating all weights, you update only a small, low-rank matrix—mathematically a tiny update that achieves most of the improvement. The question: can we make LoRA even better?
202.wh: Standard LoRA has two technical issues. First, when the embedding dimension is large (the 'width' of the network), learning the first matrix (A) is inefficient—the random initialization doesn't help the gradient-based learning. Second, initializing the second matrix (B) as zeros creates a dead-weight problem: at the start, the update has no effect, and gradients have to bootstrap the learning from scratch. These inefficiencies accumulate, slowing training and limiting accuracy gains.
202.ap: LoRA-E2 makes two changes. First, it initializes the A matrix using a Gaussian distribution with a specific variance (scaled by the embedding dimension to the power -3/4). This variance scaling is chosen so that the initial random matrix neither swamps nor suppresses gradients; it's the Goldilocks zone for learning. Second, it trains the B and A matrices using the Gauss-Seidel iteration, a classical numerical method that updates them in a coordinated way, unlike standard gradient descent which updates them simultaneously.
202.ww: Proper initialization matters because it affects how quickly gradients flow into the weights at the start of training. A variance scaled to the network width ensures that the random matrix is 'compatible' with the network's scale. Gauss-Seidel updates work better than simultaneous updates because they let one matrix respond to changes in the other, creating more stable and faster convergence—it's like two dancers who take turns leading rather than both leading at once.
202.po: In practice, LoRA-E2 improves fine-tuning accuracy by 1–10% on standard benchmarks and converges 3× faster. For large models like LLaMA, this means cheaper, quicker adaptation to new tasks, with gains that matter in production systems where training time and accuracy both directly impact the bottom line.

203.bp: Many real-world data problems have partial labels: you know some objects' categories, but not all. Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) is the task of automatically classifying everything—known and unknown categories—from this partial label set. Imagine you have labeled photos of 'dog' and 'cat,' but unlabeled photos that might be 'dog,' 'cat,' or 'bird.' How do you learn to identify the birds you've never seen labeled?
203.wh: Models pre-trained on known categories (dog, cat) develop bias toward them. When the model sees a new, unknown image, it tries to fit it into known categories rather than recognizing 'this is something new.' This is particularly bad because novel categories have no labeled examples to learn from. Recent methods use pseudo-labels (guessing the category, then treating the guess as truth) and contrastive learning (learning by comparing similar and dissimilar pairs), but they lack explicit signals saying 'separate the novel categories from known ones.' The result is confusion at the boundary between known and unknown.
203.ap: This paper treats category discovery as a latent variable problem: for each unlabeled example, there's a hidden variable saying 'is this known or novel?' They use Expectation-Maximization (EM), a classic algorithm for finding hidden structure. The EM-disentangling step softly assigns each example to known or novel, then uses that assignment to guide learning. They also apply dual contrastive objectives: pull examples of the same novel category together, and push apart ambiguous examples near the decision boundary. A consistency regularization ensures the model generalizes.
203.ww: EM works here because it's designed to recover hidden structure from data. By modeling 'known vs. novel' as a latent variable, you can explicitly separate them rather than hoping they emerge. The dual contrastive objectives work because they directly target the confusion: novel categories are pulled together so they cluster, while boundary cases are pushed apart so the decision is clean.
203.po: The framework improves category discovery accuracy by reducing misclassification of novel categories. Crucially, it makes the disentanglement explicit—the model learns to separate known from novel categories as part of training, not as a side effect. This matters in open-world scenarios like image retrieval or recommendation systems, where new categories constantly emerge.

204.bp: AI systems are deployed in critical domains—medical diagnosis, autonomous vehicles, financial decisions—where security matters enormously. When an AI system is vulnerable to attack (e.g., adversarial inputs fooling the model, data poisoning, model extraction), how do we know? Security analysts must connect vulnerability findings from different tools, research papers, and organizational standards (NIST, OWASP, ISO). Today, this process is mostly manual and error-prone because each security tool speaks its own language.
204.wh: Security analysis tools produce different outputs with different terminology and concepts. One tool says 'adversarial example detected,' another says 'model robustness issue,' a third says 'input validation missing.' Analysts manually correlate these reports with mitigation knowledge scattered across MITRE ATLAS (adversarial tactics), OWASP (web security), NIST (standards), ISO (governance). This takes time, introduces human error, and doesn't scale to the number of AI systems being deployed.
204.ap: AI SecOnto proposes an ontology—a structured, machine-readable representation of AI security knowledge. An ontology is like a master dictionary that defines every security concept and how they relate (e.g., 'adversarial example' is a type of 'input attack,' which requires 'input validation' mitigation). The framework ingests raw vulnerability findings from security tools and translates them into this common ontology (like converting multiple languages to a universal semantic language). Analysts can then query the ontology: 'show all vulnerabilities affecting model robustness in this MLOps pipeline' and get structured mitigation recommendations automatically.
204.ww: Ontologies work here because security knowledge has deep structure—concepts relate to each other in ways that matter for analysis. By formalizing that structure once, automated queries become possible. Every new vulnerability finding automatically maps to the broader security knowledge base, reducing manual work and catching patterns humans might miss.
204.po: The prototype demonstrates query-driven vulnerability assessment and structured mitigation for MLOps pipelines. Instead of analysts manually reading reports and cross-referencing standards, the system correlates findings automatically and surfaces mitigations, scaling security analysis to match the deployment rate of AI systems.

205.bp: Recommender systems decide what you see on Netflix or Spotify. Classical approaches build a graph (you → movie, movie → genre, etc.) or use pure text descriptions. Large language models (LLMs) have vast world knowledge: they know that 'The Matrix' is sci-fi action about AI, ideal for someone who liked 'Blade Runner.' The question: how do you combine LLMs (which understand semantics) with interaction graphs (which capture your actual behavior) to recommend better?
205.wh: LLM-based recommenders know item features well but ignore user-item interaction patterns—who watched what together, which users are similar. Graphs capture interactions but require explicit encoding; LLMs don't naturally ingest graph structure. Fusing the two is hard because they're heterogeneous: graph embeddings (compressed representations of nodes) are different from LLM token embeddings, making them hard to align.
205.ap: GALRec uses a strategy called GAL-tuning, which combines two components. A graph encoder processes user-item interactions and extracts collaborative signals (users like me enjoyed these items). An LLM predictor generates recommendations from textual item descriptions and context. To bridge them, they introduce GAL-alignment: graph-to-LLM alignment (adjust graph representations to match LLM space) and LLM-to-graph alignment (adjust LLM output to reflect graph patterns). The alignment minimizes the gap between what the graph 'says' and what the LLM 'says,' tuning them to agree.
205.ww: Alignment works because even though graphs and LLMs represent information differently, they're both trying to answer the same question: 'what's this user likely to enjoy?' By forcing them to agree (minimizing divergence), you let each component's strengths (graph has interaction ground truth, LLM has semantic understanding) reinforce the other.
205.po: The result is a recommender that leverages both collaborative patterns and semantic understanding, improving recommendation accuracy. For systems with sparse interaction data, the LLM component provides world knowledge; for data-rich systems, the graph component ensures recommendations match actual user behavior.

206.bp: In chemistry, biology, and software engineering, objects are often represented as bags of graphs: a molecule as multiple structural views (atoms, bonds, functional groups), a protein as interaction networks from different data sources, a software codebase as multiple dependency graphs. The question: how do you learn embeddings (compressed representations) of these multi-graph objects when you have few or no labels?
206.wh: Standard graph neural networks are designed for single graphs; extending them to bags of graphs faces three challenges. First, producing discriminative representations of the whole bag (not just individual graphs) is unclear—combining multiple graph embeddings risks losing information. Second, contrastive learning typically operates at one level (e.g., comparing individual graph embeddings), but bags have hierarchical structure (graphs within bags, sub-structures within graphs)—you need cross-hierarchical alignment. Third, standard data augmentation (adding noise or dropping edges) can destroy important graph structures or semantic meaning, hurting learning.
206.ap: HGBN (Hierarchical Graph-Bag-Network) addresses these with three components. An asymmetric hierarchical graph neural network learns representations at two levels: individual graph-level embeddings and the bag-level embedding (which aggregates graphs carefully). Cross-hierarchical contrastive objectives align graph and bag representations: pull close the bag-level embedding and its constituent graphs, and push apart bags with different structures. The augmentation strategy is structure-aware: instead of random noise, it augments in ways that preserve the graphs' semantic meaning (e.g., reordering graphs within a bag, not breaking individual graphs).
206.ww: Hierarchical representations work because bags-of-graphs have two levels of structure; capturing both levels improves downstream performance. Cross-hierarchical contrastive learning works because aligning graphs with their parent bag forces both levels to encode consistent information. Structure-aware augmentation works because semantic information is preserved, so the model learns robust features rather than brittle statistical shortcuts.
206.po: The framework enables self-supervised learning on bags of graphs without labels, with hierarchical representations that capture both individual and aggregate structure. This is valuable in chemistry (molecule property prediction from multiple structural views) and bioinformatics (protein function from interaction networks) where labeled data is scarce.

207.bp: Cities face a new challenge: electric vehicles charging at scale will stress power grids, but vehicles could also become mobile batteries (Vehicle-to-Grid or V2G), stabilizing grids during peak demand. Understanding this coupling requires simulating traffic (when do people drive?) and power grids (when is demand high?) together. But complex simulations are hard to visualize and experiment with, so decisions remain theoretical rather than empirical.
207.wh: Real-time coupled simulations of power and traffic are complex: routing affects grid load, grid events (blackouts) affect traffic, and cascading failures can spiral. Current tools require specialized software, run offline, and produce abstract numbers, not intuitive visuals. Policymakers and educators can't easily experiment with scenarios like 'what if we deploy V2G on this grid during a heatwave?' without months of work.
207.ap: Sumo×PyPSA is a web-based platform combining two simulators: SUMO (for traffic) and PyPSA (for power grids). It runs in a browser (no installation needed) and provides live visualization of Manhattan's actual infrastructure (8 substations, 15 transmission lines, 3,481 traffic signals, real street layout). Users interact with the visualization to trigger events (disable a substation, route vehicles to provide grid support) and watch cascading dynamics unfold in real-time. Four pre-built scenarios (heatwave cascades, V2G emergency response, manual recovery, custom scenarios) demonstrate the coupling.
207.ww: Browser-based real-time simulation works because commodity hardware is now fast enough, and WebSocket (a technology for live data streaming) enables instant feedback. Real data (OpenStreetMap, NYC traffic signals, power topology) makes it concrete, not abstract. Interactive exploration works because humans learn by experimenting; watching a simulation unfold is more memorable than reading a report.
207.po: Policymakers, educators, and researchers can now experiment with grid-traffic coupling interactively, observing how blackouts cascade through traffic signals and how V2G can prevent them. The platform makes complex infrastructure dynamics accessible and intuitive, enabling better decision-making about urban resilience.

208.bp: Cryptocurrencies like Ethereum are pseudonymous: your wallet address isn't your name, but all transactions are public on the blockchain. This is useful for criminals: if you steal funds (exploit a smart contract bug), you can transfer them across wallets, but observers can trace the flow. The question: how do criminals move money around after a theft to mix it into the legitimate economy without being caught? Understanding their patterns helps design detection systems.
208.wh: Most work on blockchain crime focuses on detecting stolen funds quickly (flag the wallet address) or identifying laundering accounts (find the mixer service). But behavioral patterns underlying how criminals actually launder money remain opaque. What do their transfer sequences look like? How quickly do they move funds? Do they spread money widely or concentrate it? These patterns aren't well studied, so detection systems might miss a key signal.
208.ap: This paper reconstructs token flows from exploiter-controlled addresses by tracing on-chain transactions. For each flow, they compute behavioral metrics: financial trajectory (how much value moves over time), temporal dynamics (how fast do transfers happen, are there delays?), structural topology (is the transfer graph a simple line or a complex tree?), and value dispersion (does the criminal spread funds across many wallets or keep them together?). They then empirically describe the patterns they observe across real exploits.
208.ww: Behavioral metrics work because human criminal behavior isn't perfectly random. Constraints like 'moving too fast attracts attention,' 'spreading too widely loses track,' and 'institutional requirements (like KYC) force certain patterns' shape real laundering. By measuring these constraints empirically, you expose the patterns that detection systems can learn to recognize.
208.po: The result is a behavioral profile of post-exploit laundering: rapid fund movement, shallow transfer structures, and broad dispersion. These patterns exhibit measurable regularities—meaning they can be incorporated into detection frameworks. Instead of watching for specific wallet addresses (which criminals can evade by changing wallets), detection can watch for behavioral anomalies, making it harder to launder stolen funds on Ethereum.

209.bp: Sending secret messages covertly (steganography) is valuable: political prisoners, journalists in hostile countries, security researchers in adversarial situations. The challenge: hide a large image inside something innocuous that travels openly. QR codes are perfect: they're everywhere (payment systems, packages, advertisements), and no one suspects them of hiding secrets. But how do you compress a large image into the tiny data region of a QR code while recovering it perfectly, and making the recovered image look realistic (not blocky or corrupted)?
209.wh: Traditional steganography embeds data in images, and security relies on disguising statistical properties (the hidden data shouldn't change pixel statistics in detectable ways). But compressing a large image into a QR code requires ~400× compression; you can't just hide data, you must transform it radically. Traditional methods would produce artifacts (blockiness) that either look unnatural or can't be recovered. Moreover, adversaries can attack transmission (degrade the QR code's quality), and pixel-based methods break under any noise.
209.ap: DiSCoQR uses diffusion models (generative models that learn to reverse corruption) combined with semantic compression. Instead of compressing pixel data directly, they extract the semantic information (what the image is, conceptually) and encode that into binary form (1s and 0s). The diffusion model learns to recognize this semantic code and reconstruct a realistic image that matches it. The binary code integrates seamlessly into a standard QR code's data region. The key: the reconstructed image isn't pixel-identical to the original, but it's semantically equivalent—it conveys the same information and works for downstream tasks.
209.ww: Semantic compression works here because you don't need pixel-perfect recovery; you need functional equivalence (the image still communicates its meaning). Diffusion models are good at this because they're trained to generate realistic images from noisy or compressed input—they handle the reconstruction naturally. The QR container is robust because error-correcting codes in QR (built-in redundancy) can handle some quality degradation; semantic equivalence means degradation doesn't break the message.
209.po: The result achieves 400× compression while maintaining semantic quality—a secret image travels inside an innocent QR code, and on recovery, it's realistic enough to serve its purpose (viewing, analysis, etc.). This enables covert communication through ubiquitous, undetectable channels, important for privacy in hostile environments.
